# Performance And Scaling

**Example status — runnable compiler workflow:** the compilation example trains
and predicts from Arrow inputs; the other sections describe tuning choices.

RelFlow performance is determined by the schema shape as much as by model
width. Fixed branch lengths, datatype capacities, data-loader behavior, and
prediction output can dominate before raw parameter count does.

Treat every throughput number as workload-specific. Record the schema, input
length distribution, hardware, precision, batch size, software version, and
output configuration next to the result.

## Measure The Whole Path

Separate four measurements:

| Measurement | Includes | Use it to diagnose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data preparation | Arrow scan, batch preprocessing, structural query, ragged coalescing, vocabulary/normalizer work | Storage layout, source binding, nested transforms, and Arrow kernel cost. |
| Encode + forward | Tensorization and model execution | Branch lengths, datatype capacity, model width/depth, device utilization. |
| Write/postprocess | CPU transfer, typed Arrow construction, embeddings, top-k, reshaping | Oversized output contracts and unnecessary retained columns. |
| End-to-end service | Queue, dynamic batching, all stages above, JSON, network | User-visible latency and saturation. |

Lightning runs include RelFlow's `throughput/train`, `throughput/validate`,
`throughput/test`, or `throughput/predict` epoch metric. It estimates processed
observations from completed batches and configured model batch size. Use it for
comparisons under the same setup, then confirm important results with an
external end-to-end measurement.

Train, validation, and test throughput use Lightning's module-metric path.
Prediction has no Lightning result collection, so `throughput/predict` is kept
on the `ThroughputLogger` callback and sent directly to an attached logger; do
not expect it in `trainer.callback_metrics`.

## Control Repeated Context First

Every `Branch(length=...)` reserves a fixed number of positions. Short records
are padded; long records are truncated or rejected according to `overflow`.
For attention-enabled branches, work also grows with interactions among local
positions.

Before increasing a branch length:

1. measure the observed length distribution by split;
2. choose a percentile or business rule, not the maximum outlier;
3. select `overflow="head"` or `"tail"` from event meaning;
4. log truncation outside RelFlow if losing records matters operationally;
5. compare quality and throughput at two or three candidate lengths.

Nested branches multiply shape. A long child inside a long parent can create a
large padded tensor even when most observations are sparse. Window, filter, or
summarize irrelevant events in a preprocessor before expanding model capacity.

### Automatic Token Packing

Sparse branch and coordinate encoders automatically gather present tokens before
normalization, query/key/value projections, attention, and feed-forward layers.
Rows with equal live lengths share an attention call. Original token positions
and row boundaries are retained, and outputs return to their structural slots
before pooling and routing. Every present token remains available; model
capacity, parameters, objectives, and checkpoint names stay the same.

Packing needs no configuration. Fully occupied sequences, active training
dropout, and encoder modules with hooks or custom implementations retain dense
execution. Evaluation can use packing even when training dropout is configured.
Data tensors and pooling still have padded shapes, so configured branch lengths
continue to affect memory. Benefits depend on occupancy, batch size, and the
number of distinct sequence lengths.

Packing changes floating-point operation order. Compare training and held-out
behavior when changing occupancy or shape; checkpoint compatibility does not
guarantee the same floating-point training trajectory.

When every processed row contains at least one present token, branch encoding
and attention pooling also avoid redundant row copies and zero-filled output
initialization. Rows may still contain padding. Outputs retain independent
storage for custom modules and callbacks, and this optimization needs no setting.

## Size Width And Depth

- `d_model` widens datatype embeddings, projections, attention, pooling, and
  decoders across the entire tree.
- Branches with multiple direct leaf fields use one coordinate-local attention
  block before their sequence encoder. It follows the branch attention mode,
  head count, and dropout.
- `n_layers` adds sequential self-attention blocks to the branch sequence
  encoder after that coordinate-local block.
- `reduction=rf.Attention(n_layers=...)` adds learned-query reduction blocks;
  each block also contains a feed-forward network.
- Attention `n_outputs` increases both the reduction output and the sequence
  routed into the parent.
- `reduction=None` routes every encoded child slot with its presence state and
  can make a parent's sequence much larger than any fixed output count.
- `dropout` may improve generalization but does not reduce inference cost.

Increase width only after verifying the input contract and observing
underfitting. Increase depth only after a width comparison. Use
`sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())` for parameter size, but profile
representative activations because repeated context often controls memory.

## Compare Attention Modes

`mha`, `gqa`, and `mqa` share the same query-head count. GQA uses half as many
key/value heads (minimum one); MQA uses one. This reduces key/value projection
width, but local attention still considers the same positions.

`attention="none"` removes the branch's self-attention stack while retaining
its independently configured reduction. With the default `rf.Attention()`,
learned-query attention still runs. It is useful for short branches, low-cost
baselines, or testing whether pre-reduction cross-position interaction adds
value.

Benchmark each mode on the intended PyTorch version and accelerator. Kernel
support and shape can matter more than theoretical parameter savings.

## Budget The Reduction Route

Branch reduction changes both information capacity and the shape seen by the
parent:

| Reduction | Approximate local reduction work | Parent tokens |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| `rf.Attention(n_outputs=Q)` | Proportional to `Q × L` per reduction layer | `Q` per branch coordinate |
| `rf.Mean()` | Linear in `L` | `1` per branch coordinate |
| `None` | No reduction module | All `L` encoded tokens per branch coordinate |

Here `L` is the branch's assembled child-memory length, not merely
`Branch.length`. Child fields contribute field-major token segments, and child
Branch outputs contribute their own segments.

`None` saves local reduction work but is not automatically cheaper. Those
tokens move to the parent, whose self-attention remains quadratic in its total
sequence length. Nested pass-through branches can therefore multiply activation
memory and compute. Measure the complete tree rather than timing the child in
isolation.

The cheapest reduction can also be the wrong model. Mean directly retains only
the average encoded vector; the preceding self-attention would have to encode
cardinality, identity, extrema, order, or item-specific statistics before that
average. More learned outputs retain additional latent capacity but do not
perform keyed joins. A downstream one-output reduction can erase the extra
capacity immediately. Profile paired configurations that differ only in the
reduction, and retain a synthetic behavior check for any relationship the
application depends on.

## Budget Datatype Capacity

### Category And Set

Category and Set content storage grows with `size × d_model`, and decoding or
scoring grows with `size`. A fixed-width projection elsewhere in a decoder does
not make a large vocabulary free.

- choose capacity from expected distinct training labels plus explicit
  headroom;
- monitor Category `vocabulary.size` by address;
- investigate capacity warnings rather than silently increasing every field;
- use `Hash` when identifier equality matters without a learned vocabulary;
- keep high-cardinality join identifiers as metadata when they are not a model
  feature;
- avoid large `topk` output unless consumers use it.

### Text And Vector

Text cost depends on tokenizer/model choice and configured token length; it also
requires the `text` extra. Vector cost grows with source vector width and the
projection into `d_model`. Measure transfer and parsing as well as forward time
when vectors arrive from another service.

`Text` groups valued rows by attended length and removes trailing right padding
inside each frozen-encoder microbatch. `max_length` still controls truncation
and storage, and unusually long rows can still determine a microbatch's cost.
Tune `tokenizer_batch_size`, `encoder_batch_size`, and `max_length` from the
observed row and token-length distributions. `tokenizer_batch_size` bounds
transient Python strings at the Hugging Face boundary; `encoder_batch_size`
bounds frozen-model forward passes. Left-padded tokenizers conservatively retain
their full width.

## Feed The Accelerator

Measure worker count and pinning together. Encoding, interprocess transfer and
worker startup can exceed the saved device-transfer time, particularly for
small in-memory batches. Storage-bound datasets may benefit from different
settings.

For small in-memory work, `ArrowDataModule` with a `pa.Table` removes file
discovery and remote I/O from the experiment. For file-backed jobs, pass paths
or use `rf.source(...)`. Selection stays lazy and workers open their own readers;
consumers currently replay source I/O and preprocessing.

Important controls include:

- `num_workers`: CPU preparation workers per distributed rank;
- `persistent_workers`: avoids recreating worker-local filesystems and scanners
  each epoch;
- `prefetch_factor`: bounds prepared batches waiting per worker;
- Dataset fragment and Parquet row-group layout: determine decode and remote
  read granularity;
- `pin_memory`: recursively pins encoded tensors for accelerator transfer;
- `shuffle_rows`: larger streaming buffers improve mixing but consume memory;
- `sample`: useful for bounded experiments, not a substitute for a valid
  split.

Measure loader iteration, device transfer and the complete training step
together when tuning these controls. With `num_workers=0`, pinning runs inside
loader iteration; faster GPU copies may not repay that CPU cost. Workers move
preparation off the training thread but add interprocess delivery and queueing.
Increase workers or prefetch depth only when the complete pipeline improves.

GPU transfers already use TensorDict's nonblocking CUDA path. Overlapping a
future batch's copy with computation additionally requires pinned buffers,
separate streams and correct buffer lifetimes; a nonblocking flag alone does
not establish overlap. Input-only Number, Boolean, Hash, Text, Category and
Vector fields omit unused reconstruction targets. This reduces retained and
transferred payloads; the benefit depends on datatype and input width.
Category still performs its regularization draws to preserve the training
random-number sequence.

Run a data-only or CPU baseline when the accelerator is idle. If increasing
batch size does not improve device utilization, the bottleneck may be
preprocessing, explicit queries, tensorization, or I/O.

## Understand Ragged Preparation

RelFlow eagerly coalesces every encoded address for a processed Arrow batch
before any datatype codec runs. Fields do not each recursively walk Python
records. The shared path owns missing versus null, branch overflow, padding,
final `Tokens` state, and dense placement. Each extension
enforces its declared Arrow terminal compatibility families; the ragged core
does not name concrete leaf types. Datatype codecs still perform inherently
field-specific work such as vocabulary updates, date parsing, hashing, or
tokenization after overflow selects retained values.

Direct selection is the default when a node's `query` is `None`. Explicit
node-relative structural queries are parsed once, bind against an Arrow schema,
and execute columnarly. RelFlow walks each active schema branch once per model
batch. A branch's query, retained records, overflow decision, shape, and dense
placement are shared by all active descendants; each leaf evaluates only its
node-relative selector and builds its own null/value state. All `RaggedField`
objects are ready before the first datatype codec runs. Do not add queries that
merely restate schema names.

Arrow compute kernels and NumPy offset/placement operations perform this
shared structural work; there is no RelFlow JIT switch to enable. A
preprocessor can dominate when it calls Python once per value.
Prefer column expressions and whole ragged collection transforms, measure them
separately, and increase the model batch only within the memory budget. Polars
converts once at ingress; profile that boundary when frames are large.

## Use Precision And Batch Size Deliberately

Configure numerical precision and accumulation on Lightning's `Trainer`. Start
with a batch that fits comfortably, then increase while watching memory,
throughput, and validation behavior.

Larger batches can improve device utilization but change the number of optimizer
updates per epoch. Preserve effective optimization conditions when comparing
throughput experiments—for example by controlling learning rate, accumulation,
and total update count.

Mixed precision can reduce activation memory on supported accelerators. Validate
numeric behavior for each datatype and loss rather than assuming identical
quality.

Compare inference precision separately, including output conversion and
serialization in the measurement. Validate the resulting predictions as well
as latency.

## Compile Encoder And Pool Regions

Call `model.compile()` before training or prediction to compile branch encoder
stacks and learned attention pools, including decoder pools. It changes the
existing model and returns that same instance, so it can follow the constructor.
Lightning continues to own device placement and the training loop.

This small example checks the complete workflow. Use representative training
and held-out data when evaluating performance or model quality.

```{python .marimo}
#| echo: true
#| output: true

import lightning.pytorch as lit
import pyarrow as pa
import torch

import relflow as rf
from relflow.helpers.optimizers import adamw

torch.manual_seed(7)
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
records = pa.table(
    {"amount": [2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0], "label": [False, False, True, True]}
)
model = rf.Model(
    d_model=16,
    n_layers=1,
    n_heads=4,
    batch_size=4,
    optimizer=adamw(learning_rate=1e-3),
    amount=rf.Number,
    label=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
).compile()
datamodule = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    model=model,
    train=records,
    validate=records,
    num_workers=0,
    persistent_workers=False,
    pin_memory=False,
)
trainer = lit.Trainer(
    accelerator=device,
    devices=1,
    max_epochs=1,
    limit_train_batches=1,
    limit_val_batches=1,
    num_sanity_val_steps=0,
    logger=False,
    enable_checkpointing=False,
    enable_progress_bar=False,
    enable_model_summary=False,
)
trainer.fit(model=model, datamodule=datamodule)

# Lightning may move the model to CPU when its loop finishes.
observations = records.drop(["label"])
predictions = model.to(device).predict(observations)
print(predictions.column_names)
```

### Select Regions

The two Boolean switches are independent. Every call replaces the previous
selection and compiler settings; omitted switches return to their defaults.

```python
assert model.compile(encoders=True, pools=False) is model  # Only encoder stacks.
model.compile(encoders=False, pools=True)                  # Only attention pools.
model.compile()                                           # Both; default settings.
model.compile(encoders=False, pools=False)                 # Disable compilation.
```

`encoders` covers branch sequence encoder stacks. `pools` covers learned-query
attention reduction in branches and decoders; it does not include mean pooling.
Coordinate encoders, tensorfield operations, routing, packing preparation,
losses and metrics keep their existing paths. Custom compute overrides and
customized regions run eagerly. Nested hooks also make the affected region run
eagerly, including hooks added after compilation.

### Compiler Settings And Warmup

`backend="inductor"`, `dynamic=None`, and `options=None` are the defaults.
`backend` accepts a PyTorch backend name or callable. `dynamic=None` lets
PyTorch adapt to changing shapes; `True` requests dynamic shapes from the first
trace, and `False` specializes shapes. Some operations still require
specialization. Backend-specific `options` override RelFlow's defaults.

```python
model.compile(encoders=True, pools=True, dynamic=True, options={})
```

The Inductor defaults preserve eager random draws and disable CUDA graphs and
automatic tensor padding. Every selected region uses `fullgraph=True`.
Unsupported graph operations or backend errors surface during setup or first
execution; they are not silently replaced by eager execution. Select one region
family at a time to isolate a failure. `backend="eager"` is useful for checking
graph capture without Inductor code generation; it is not a speed setting.
See [PyTorch's compiler API](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.12/generated/torch.compile.html)
for backend options and dynamic-shape behavior.

Compilation happens lazily on real inputs. Initial training, validation and
prediction can compile different graphs; new shapes, devices or dtypes can
trigger more compilation. Warm up the actual mode and representative batch
shapes before measuring steady throughput, and report startup separately.
When timing CUDA from Python, synchronize before starting and after completing
the measured work. Compare complete training steps or public prediction calls,
including data preparation and output writing when those belong to your use
case. Keep the data, seed, optimizer, precision and update budget matched, and
compare held-out behavior: compiled floating-point results can differ.

### Evaluate The Incremental Gain

Inductor is already the backend used by `model.compile()`. RelFlow compiles
encoder stacks and attention pools as separate regions; `fullgraph=True`
applies to each region, not the entire training step. Embedding, routing,
losses, metrics and optimizer execution remain outside those compiled regions.
Compare the same optimized model with and without compilation to measure its
contribution. Gains from token packing, reduced transfers and fused AdamW also
appear in a cumulative comparison against an older release.

In September 2026 validation on an RTX 3090 with PyTorch 2.12.0, FP32 and three
seeds, the incremental steady-throughput results were:

| Workload | Compilation versus the same model running eagerly |
|---|---:|
| Training, equal weight across 12 shared scenarios | +2.3% |
| Prediction, equal weight across 8 scenarios | -0.4% |
| Sparse-history training, batch 128 and width 512 | +10.0% |
| Sparse-history prediction, batch 128 and width 512 | +11.0% |

These are geometric means of paired throughput ratios, using each run's
arithmetic mean latency after warmup and retaining every measured interval.
The scenario averages include an empty-history case that executes no compiled
regions; they do not represent a production workload mix. The comparison used
the public defaults, with CUDA graphs and automatic compiler padding disabled.

Compilation remains optional and workload-dependent. In the 64-output case,
compilation increased prediction latency by 12.6% versus eager execution on the
same optimized model. Long training sessions amortize compilation startup;
they do not remove a steady-execution regression. Evaluate training and
prediction separately, and use the region switches to measure encoder and pool
compilation independently on the actual schema.

Prediction tolerance checks and the selected learning proofs passed, while
strict training-state and loss-trajectory comparisons showed numerical drift.
Those checks do not establish identical training quality. Larger compilation
regions or more aggressive Inductor autotuning require separate measurements;
the default comparison does not establish their benefit.

### Save, Load And Resume

Compilation is runtime state, not checkpoint configuration. A newly loaded
model is eager even if its saved model was compiled. Load and place the model,
then select compilation explicitly:

```python
model.save("model.ckpt")
restored = rf.Model.load("model.ckpt").to(device).compile()
restored_predictions = restored.predict(observations)
```

`reset_contracts()`, successful schema mutations and checkpoint rebuilds such
as `restore_checkpoint_state(...)` clear compilation. Deep copies and pickle
round trips also start eager. Reapply `.compile(...)` afterward, outside active
Lightning loops.

Native Lightning resume into an existing model behaves differently: select
compilation before `trainer.fit(model, datamodule=..., ckpt_path=...)`, and
loading its weights retains that explicit selection. The checkpoint never
enables compilation by itself. Use a Lightning training checkpoint when you
need to resume optimizer and loop state; see
[Training With Lightning](lightning.qmd#select-and-restore-checkpoints).

## Compare Optimizer Implementations

The AdamW factory uses PyTorch's fused implementation by default, preserving
its existing parameter groups and weight-decay rules:

```python
from relflow.helpers.optimizers import adamw

model.optimizer = adamw(learning_rate=1e-3)
```

Pass `fused=None` for PyTorch's automatic selection or `fused=False` to disable
fusion. Fused arithmetic can produce different floating-point training
trajectories. Compare complete training steps on the intended device: a large
improvement in optimizer time
can have a small effect when forward and backward dominate. The available
settings are described in the [PyTorch AdamW documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.12/generated/torch.optim.AdamW.html).

For checkpoint resume with gradient scaling, construct the helper with the
saved `fused` setting. Optimizer checkpoints made with the previous helper
default need `adamw(learning_rate=1e-3, fused=None)`; loading them into an
optimizer constructed with `fused=True` can fail in PyTorch's `GradScaler`.

## Distributed Training

::: {.callout-note title="Arrow scheduler"}
The Arrow-native data module combines distributed rank and local worker identity
into one deterministic consumer index. All sources replay the global stream
for disjoint ownership. File manifests are frozen before workers start, but
source-native fragment scheduling remains deferred.
:::

Measure repeated source reads when tuning worker count, especially on remote
storage. Increasing workers can increase I/O without increasing throughput.

For an ordered preprocessor pipeline, time each stage separately as well as the
complete tuple. A partition-scoped stage streams its outputs into the next;
each dataset-scoped stage is a full materialization barrier at its exact tuple
position. Moving that barrier changes both memory and semantics, so RelFlow
never reorders stages. Record processor order, scope, input rows, emitted rows,
and Arrow schemas with a preprocessing benchmark.

## Optimize Prediction Output

Keep Arrow output through downstream operations that accept it. Conversion to
Python values and JSON serialization can dominate after model execution
becomes faster; measure them separately from Arrow-to-Arrow prediction.

Prediction can spend substantial time moving and serializing data:

- enable `embed=True` only at addresses consumers need;
- request only useful Category top-k values;
- retain only source fields an output consumer needs;
- use a Polars postprocessor to flatten or remove unused fields;
- use `Writer` for partitioned batch output rather than collecting a whole
  dataset in memory;
- set service `max_batch_size` and latency against the real request-size
  distribution;
- benchmark JSON backend and response schema validation separately.

When several postprocessors are installed, benchmark the ordered tuple and
each stage. Every stage receives a complete eager DataFrame; splitting one
vectorized expression into many tiny stages can make fixed dispatch and schema
validation visible at real-time batch sizes.

An online latency target and an offline throughput target usually need different
batch sizes.

## Benchmark Record

Store at least this metadata with a result:

```yaml
relflow_version: 0.4.11
device: "example: NVIDIA GPU model or CPU model"
precision: "32-true"
batch_size: 128
world_size: 1
records: 100000
branch_length_percentiles: {p50: 12, p95: 48, max_configured: 64}
d_model: 64
layers_by_branch: {record: 2, events: 1}
attention_by_branch: {record: mha, events: gqa}
reduction_by_branch: {record: "attention:4", events: "none"}
output: {targets: [label], embeddings: [record], topk: 3}
measurement_boundary: "raw parquet read through parquet prediction write"
```

The values above are a reporting template, not a benchmark result.

## Failure Signals

| Signal | Diagnostic | Likely fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accelerator utilization is low | Time read/each preprocess stage/encode separately from forward | Simplify or combine the measured bottleneck, remove an unnecessary dataset barrier, or fix remote I/O before widening the model. |
| Memory is high with mostly short histories | Compare observed lengths with configured branch shapes | Shorten/window branches or choose a justified overflow policy. |
| Parent memory jumps after enabling pass-through | Inspect child `reduction=None` and the assembled parent sequence | Restore a bounded reduction, shorten the branch, or budget the larger parent attention when token-level evidence is required. |
| Quality collapses as branch length grows | Compare reduction output count, pass-through, and downstream bottlenecks | Preserve more child outputs and ensure a parent does not immediately collapse them; verify with a paired behavior proof. |
| More ranks do not improve throughput | Check ownership, remote I/O, worker multiplication, and synchronization time | Correct sharding and remove the serial bottleneck before adding ranks. |
| Prediction is slower than training forward | Measure CPU conversion, top-k, embeddings, postprocessing, and writes | Narrow the output contract and use partitioned `Writer` output. |
| Callback throughput disagrees with load tests | Compare measurement boundaries and partial final batches | Publish both callback and end-to-end measurements with their exact boundaries. |
